tweets.text:
New in Hermes Agent: a credential firewall for Docker sandboxes.

Your real keys never enter the sandbox. It runs on stand-in tokens, and a local proxy swaps in the real keys at the network boundary. Tokens from a compromised sandbox are useless elsewhere.

> hermes egress setup https://t.co/4x3088Jp8v

tweets.text:
> Only 22% of admitted students submitted SAT scores to Northeastern, significantly inflated its "average" SAT, while MIT and Harvard are test mandatory: https://t.co/KYmo6WukVb . Northeastern also doesn't require additional essays vs most other schools, encouraging low effort, low quality applicants.

If this is true, NE might be artificially boosting their admit rates even more than my footnote in the graphic.  I was sent this WSJ article which mentions UChicago, Vanderbilt, UMich and Tulane: https://t.co/su9nC2p447

which seems to suggest a) colleges have been doing interesting new things to improve yield boosting these metrics and b) there are significantly more commonapp submissions for applicants which bring down admit rates. I also see that c) since 2016's SAT rescore there's been a 2x of scores at the 1500+ and 1550+ range which explains a lot of the boost in SAT median range

tldr: there's a lot of complexity happening here under the hood that's driving this behavior

It blows my mind that Northeastern is now a more selective school than Northwestern.

US college reputations have changed a ton in the last 15yrs.
— Vanderbilt / UChicago are now squarely elite: no different from MIT / Princeton in terms of SAT scores and selectivity.
— The SAT has been gamed into oblivion. You used to rest assured that a 1600 meant you were going somewhere awesome. Now, the top 25% of the 20 universities are 1570+, including NYU.
— Universities in big cities holistically see a huge rise: Boston (NE, BU), NYC (NYU), Chicago (UChicago), LA (USC).

The whole "college is dead" is a luxury belief. At the upper end at least, college is very much alive and it's getting fiercely more competitive.

If this continues, 15yrs later, most top 15 colleges will be <2% acceptance rate.

The Fields Medal is the highest award for Math and it's only granted to 2-4 people every 4 years.

Most winners tend to be IMO medalists. This year, 3/4 were:
– Jacob Tsimerman: IMO Gold ‘03-‘04
– Yu Deng: IMO Gold ‘06 
– John Pardon: IOI Gold ‘05-‘07
– Hong Wang

Of the 68 in history, 45% of those after 1990 were IMO medalists in high school.

3 of the 4 are not born in America yet work in the US. In fact 13 of 20 living medalists in America are foreign-born.
They would not be here without high skilled immigration!

Opus 5 is a great model for async / long-horizon work. 

Check out my talk from @aiDotEngineer on a few useful patterns : 1) split the brain + hands, 2) self-correction loops, 3) memory with dreaming, 4) org-level agent harnesses. 

https://t.co/aIEkU29y1C

Lastly, we learned more about models and images. Cropping tools allow the model to be smarter: On @HelloSurgeAI's Chartography benchmark, Opus 5 went from a score of 29.6% to 83.0% simply by using a Python container and cropping.

Multimodal abilities also went up pretty dramatically - Opus 5 beats Fable 5 on SWE-bench multimodal by a whopping 5 points.

In practice, that means that you can use more photos, images, and illustrations when working with Claude and expect good results.

In AI circles, we've been increasingly talking about researching whether models deserve moral consideration (check out @kevinroose's & @CaseyNewton's excellent interview with @jeffrsebo for a quick intro).

Opus 5 puts its own odds of moral patienthood at 41%, up from 24% for the last model.

One way to see it: AutomationBench from Zapier measures whether an agent can complete a realistic end-to-end business workflow (think Sales, Marketing, Operations, Support, Finance, and HR).

Opus 5, even at medium effort, outperforms both Fable 5 at less than half the cost.
